pedagogy.summary: Children move from 'which is longer?' to 'how much longer?' — measuring both objects in the same standard unit and subtracting the smaller from the larger to give the difference expressed with its unit ('7 cm longer'). This is the additive-comparison (difference-unknown) structure applied to measured lengths, and it is best made visible as the overhang between two bars aligned at a common baseline.
bestPractices: Measure both objects in the same unit first, then find the difference by subtracting the smaller from the larger.
Demand the amount, not just the direction: the answer is '7 cm taller', not 'the shelf is taller'.
Make the difference visible — align the two lengths at a common baseline (bar model / number line) so the overhang IS the difference.
Use comparison ('difference unknown') word problems and represent them with tape/bar diagrams and an equation with the unknown.
Keep both measures in one unit before subtracting; expose the error of subtracting across different units.
keyRepresentations: Two bars aligned at a common baseline with the overhang marked as the difference
A number line showing both lengths from 0 and the gap between their endpoints
A tape/bar 'comparison' diagram with the difference as the missing part
An equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (32 + ? = 45)
commonMisconceptions: Gives only the comparison ('the shelf is taller') without quantifying by how much.
Subtracts the wrong way or mis-subtracts, or compares by lining objects up with mismatched endpoints.
Compares the bare numbers when the two measures are in different units (shelf in m, desk in cm).
Treats the difference as the sum, or adds when the problem asks how much longer.

learn.summary: Children move from 'which is longer?' to 'how much longer?' — measuring both objects in the same standard unit and subtracting the smaller from the larger to state the difference WITH its unit ('7 cm taller'). This is the additive-comparison (difference-unknown) structure applied to measured lengths, made visible as the overhang between two lengths aligned at a common baseline.

activities.title: How much taller? Measure, align, and find the overhang
feedback: If the learner answers only 'the bookshelf is taller' with no number, point to the overhang above the shorter object's top and ask 'how much is this extra bit?' so the difference becomes a quantity.
If the learner subtracts larger-from-smaller or lines objects up with unequal starting points, re-align both at a common baseline/zero and read the gap; then subtract smaller from larger.
Confirm a full answer states the difference with its unit and can be shown as the overhang on the bar model or number line.
activities.rationale: Aligning both lengths at a common baseline turns the abstract 'difference' into a visible, measurable overhang, matching the difference-unknown comparison structure; measuring and expressing with a unit (2.MD.4) and representing with tape/number-line diagrams and an unknown-symbol equation (2.MD.5–6) are the grade-level targets.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.

Length addition/subtraction problems (2.MD.5) are represented with drawings of rulers, tape or number-bond diagrams, and equations with a symbol for the unknown; a number line diagram is a measurement model in which consecutive whole numbers are one unit apart, so children reason about distances between positions.
Year 3 pupils measure, compare, add and subtract lengths and solve 'how much longer/taller' comparison problems, expressing the difference in standard units.
learnerActions: Place two objects of clearly different height/length (e.g. a desk and a bookshelf) so both stand on the SAME baseline, with a ruler, metre stick or tape measured from zero at that baseline.
Measure both in the same unit (e.g. desk 118 cm, shelf 125 cm) and write each measurement with its unit.
Identify the strip of the longer object that sticks up above the top of the shorter one — this overhang is the answer to 'how much taller?'
Find the difference by subtracting the smaller measurement from the larger (125 − 118) and state the answer with its unit: 'the bookshelf is 7 cm taller.'

In a word-problem round, both measures are given (for example, stated in the problem's words in the same unit rather than read from the ruler), and the DIFFERENCE is the unknown: draw a comparison bar/tape diagram with two bars from a common baseline, mark the difference as the missing part, then write an equation with a symbol for the unknown difference (e.g. 32 + ? = 45, or 45 − 32 = ?) and solve it.
activities.intendedInsight: The difference is a real, measurable piece of length — the overhang between two lengths aligned at a common baseline — not just the fact that one object 'wins'. The answer must be an amount with a unit.

activities.title: Same unit first: the mixed-unit trap
feedback: If the learner writes '1 − 80' or keeps mismatched units, prompt: 'What is 1 m in centimetres?' then redo the subtraction in one unit (100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm).
Reinforce attending to the unit while measuring and whenever the two measures look different in size.
activities.rationale: A deliberate mixed-unit item exposes and corrects bare-number subtraction, a documented error; it reinforces that a difference is only meaningful in a shared unit.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.
learnerActions: Take a pair of objects measured in different units (e.g. a shelf labelled 1 m and a desk labelled 80 cm).
Before subtracting, re-express both in one common unit (e.g. 1 m = 100 cm).
Then subtract smaller from larger in that common unit and state the difference with its unit (100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm taller).
Say aloud why '1 − 80' is wrong: the numbers are in different units and cannot be subtracted as bare numbers.
activities.intendedInsight: You can only subtract lengths once they are expressed in the same unit; comparing bare numbers across different units gives a meaningless answer.

activities.title: Check questions: comparison word problems and 'by how much?'
feedback: Catch the 'names the taller one but not the amount' error by requiring a numeric answer with a unit.
If a mixed-unit item is answered by bare-number subtraction, re-express to one unit and re-solve.
activities.rationale: Response-format items can check whether the amount-with-unit and common-unit requirements are met and can surface the comparison-only and bare-number errors; such items check performance rather than build the bar-model reasoning, so pair them with the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Second graders learn to measure two objects and subtract the smaller measurement from the larger to find how much longer one object is than the other, expressing the difference in a standard length unit (2.MD.4); they can add two lengths to obtain the whole and subtract to find the difference.
learnerActions: Answer 'how much longer/taller?' items where you enter the amount (fill-in or slider), not just which object is longer.
Work at least one item that gives the two measures in different units, so you must convert to a common unit before subtracting.
For a comparison word problem, pick the correct equation with the unknown difference and justify it with a bar diagram.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct answer to a comparison problem is an amount with a unit, obtained by subtracting in a common unit — not a choice of 'which one'.

constraints: The answer must state an AMOUNT with its unit ('7 cm taller'), not just a direction ('the shelf is taller').
Both measures must be in the same unit before subtracting; subtract the smaller from the larger so the difference is positive.

To read a difference directly as a visible gap, the objects must be aligned at a common baseline/zero, because mismatched starting points produce a wrong gap. When each object is measured separately from the ruler's zero, the two measurements can be subtracted without physically lining the objects up.
A static bar-model diagram can illustrate the overhang idea but does not let the learner measure and compute across new cases; use it as a reference scaffold alongside hands-on measuring.

Recognition/selection items (choosing which is longer, or multiple choice) can check understanding but do not by themselves elicit independent measuring, subtracting and expressing — include at least one task where the learner constructs the measurement and difference.

Interactive examples (dragging objects to a shared baseline, live-shaded overhang that updates as lengths change, auto-labelled difference) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required mechanisms.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy entry rated a 3D format 'poor' ('3D adds no insight') and a conversation format 'poor' ('not a dialogue'); these are catalog fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws, and have been dropped rather than asserted as universal truths. Speaking through the reasoning can still support learning.
The legacy quiz note ('a quiz tests rather than builds the bar-model reasoning') is retained only as a scoped limitation, not as a claim that response-format items can never teach.

The mixed-unit example '1 m vs 80 cm' is used to expose the bare-number error; the correct worked value is 100 cm − 80 cm = 20 cm. The erroneous '1 − 80' appears only as something to catch, never as a valid answer in learner-facing text.

Activity 1's word-problem step was clarified so that one measure is supplied in words (not deleted) and the DIFFERENCE is the single unknown, removing an ambiguity about which quantity the bar diagram's missing part represents.
The UK National Curriculum source is verified:false in the row; it is cited for the comparison-problem framing but should not be treated as independently confirmed.

probeDeeper: You said the bookshelf is taller — by how much? Show me how you'd find that.
Where on the ruler is the 'extra bit' that makes the shelf taller than the desk?
This one is 1 m and that one is 80 cm — how much taller? Can you subtract 80 from 1?
If the desk were actually the taller one, how would your calculation change?
assess.correctAnswer: The child measures both objects in the same unit, subtracts the smaller from the larger, and states the difference WITH its unit ('the bookshelf is 7 cm taller'); for the mixed-unit pair, converts or re-expresses to a common unit before subtracting rather than comparing the bare numbers.

errorPatterns.pattern: Comparison, not difference: reports which is longer/taller but not by how much.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe with a bar model — align both at a baseline and point to the overhang; ask 'how much is the extra bit?' so the difference becomes a measurable quantity.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers 'the bookshelf is taller' or 'that one', with no number, when asked how much taller.

errorPatterns.pattern: Subtracts the wrong way or mis-subtracts / mismatched endpoints: subtracts larger-from-smaller, miscomputes, or lines the objects up with unequal starting points before comparing.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold subtracting smaller from larger and aligning both at a common baseline/zero before reading the gap; the measuring skill itself is intact.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives a nonsensical or negative-feeling difference, or eyeballs a difference from objects not aligned at the same baseline.

errorPatterns.pattern: Bare-number subtraction across different units: subtracts the numbers when the two measures are in different units (e.g. shelf 1 m, desk 80 cm -> '1 - 80').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-express both in one unit before subtracting; return to attending to the unit when measuring and choosing units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Subtracts across the mixed-unit pair without converting; keeps the numbers, drops the unit mismatch.

responseLevels.gap: Names which is longer but gives no amount, or subtracts the wrong way / across mismatched units.
responseLevels.full: Measures both in a common unit, subtracts smaller from larger, expresses the difference with its unit, converts a mixed-unit pair to a common unit first, and can show the difference as the overhang on a bar/number line.
responseLevels.partial: Finds and expresses the difference with a unit when both measures share a unit, but is caught by a mixed-unit pair or needs prompting to quantify rather than just compare.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out two objects of clearly different height/length (e.g. a desk and a bookshelf) with a metre stick or tape, and pose it as a question: 'How much taller is the bookshelf than the desk?' Then give a second pair whose measures come in different units (one labelled in metres, one in centimetres). Watch whether they measure both, subtract correctly, express the difference with a unit, and whether they attend to the units.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who grasps the difference-unknown structure gives an amount with a unit; a child who does not answers only 'the shelf is taller' (comparison, no quantity), subtracts the wrong way, or subtracts across mismatched units — each visible in what they measure and write.
